questions.stemText:
A light magnet is suspended inside a solenoid as shown in the figure below. The Earth’s magnetic flux density is $2.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T}$ and the solenoid has 20 turns and a length of 15 cm. When a current is passed through the solenoid, it is found that the magnet rotates through an angle of $68^\circ$ from its original direction.

[Top view with N, E, S and W marked. The solenoid axis runs east–west. The upper row of winding cross-sections is marked with dots and the lower row with crosses. The magnet lies across the axis with its N pole pointing north.]

What is the value of the current flowing through the solenoid?

A 0.048 A
B 0.11 A
C 0.30 A
D 2.0 A

stemImage.alt: Question 24: A light magnet is suspended inside a solenoid as shown in the figure below. The Earth’s magnetic flux density is 2.0  10−5 T and the solenoid has 20 turns and

questions.difficultyReason: The student must obtain the solenoid field from the vector triangle before calculating the current.
questions.misconception: Confusing total turns with turns per metre

explanation.body: The Earth and solenoid fields are perpendicular, so $\tan68^\circ=B_{\mathrm{solenoid}}/B_{\mathrm{Earth}}$. Thus $B_{\mathrm{solenoid}}=(2.0\times10^{-5})\tan68^\circ=4.95\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T}$. Substituting into $B_{\mathrm{solenoid}}=\mu_0nI$ gives $4.95\times10^{-5}=(4\pi\times10^{-7})(20/0.15)I$, so $I=0.30\ \mathrm{A}$.

perOption.A: Reverses the field components in the tangent ratio.
perOption.B: Uses the Earth’s field in place of the solenoid field.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses 20 turns per metre instead of 20 turns over 15 cm.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
An electron is travelling in a vacuum at speed $v$. The electron enters a region of uniform magnetic field of flux density $B$. A uniform electric field also exists in the region so that the electron remains undeflected and exits the region at point P as shown.

[In the shaded field region, magnetic field arrows point horizontally to the right. The electron enters from the lower left along a straight path sloping upwards to the right and exits at P on the top edge. The path makes angle $\theta$ with the horizontal magnetic field direction.]

The initial direction of the electron is at an angle of $\theta$ to the direction of the magnetic field.

What is the magnitude and direction of the electric field?

A. $Be\sin\theta$, into the page
B. $Be\sin\theta$, out of the page
C. $Bv\sin\theta$, into the page
D. $Bv\sin\theta$, out of the page

stemImage.alt: Question 25: An electron is travelling in a vacuum at speed v. The electron enters a region of uniform magnetic field of flux density B. A uniform electric field also exists

appearances.originalFile: grail:19926 ACJC 2025 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students must balance the force magnitudes and reverse the direction of the electric force to find the field.
questions.misconception: Confusing the electric force direction with the field direction for an electron

explanation.body: The magnetic force on the electron points out of the page and has magnitude $F_B=Bev\sin\theta$. To keep the electron undeflected, the electric force must have the same magnitude, so $E=F_E/e=Bv\sin\theta$. The electric force points into the page, so the electric field points out of the page because the electron is negatively charged.

perOption.A: Keeps the charge rather than the speed in the field magnitude and reverses the required field direction.
perOption.B: Keeps the charge rather than the speed after dividing the magnetic force by $e$.
perOption.C: Assigns the electric force direction to the field even though the electron is negatively charged.
perOption.D: Correct. The field is $Bv\sin\theta$ out of the page.

[Square PQRS has P at the upper left, Q at the upper right, R at the lower right and S at the lower left. An arrow at the centre O points to the right and is labelled resultant magnetic field.]

Due to the current in the four conductors, the resultant magnetic field at O is in the direction shown.

Which of the following must be the directions of the currents in each of the four conductors?

Option | into the page | out of the page
A | P, Q | R, S
B | P, S | Q, R

The diagram shows a bent wire in a uniform magnetic field of flux density $B$.

The length of wire in the field is $L$ and each half of the wire is inclined at an angle $\theta$ normal to the field direction. There is a current $I$ in the wire.

[Horizontal magnetic field lines point right. The current follows a bent wire from top to bottom. Two segments of length $L/2$ meet at a bend to the left of the dashed vertical line joining the entry and exit points. Each segment makes angle $\theta$ with that vertical line.]

Which row gives the magnitude and the direction of the force acting on the wire?

[Table columns in order: magnitude, direction.]

B $BIL\cos\theta$, into the page
C $BIL\sin\theta$, out of the page

questions.misconception: Using the angle to the normal directly in the sine form of the force equation.

explanation.body: Fleming’s left-hand rule gives a force out of the page. As $\theta$ tends to $0^\circ$, the wire becomes perpendicular to the field and the force is greatest. Each half contributes a perpendicular length $(L/2)\cos\theta$, so $F=BI(2)(L/2)\cos\theta=BIL\cos\theta$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Two parallel, straight conductors, placed at right angles to a ruler, carry currents of 2I and I

At which point on the ruler is the resultant magnetic field the greatest?
questions.stemText: Two parallel, straight conductors, placed at right angles to a ruler, carry currents of 2I and I flowing in opposite directions. 2I I At which point on the ruler is the resultant magnetic field the greatest? A 20 cm mark B 40 cm mark C 50 cm mark D 70 cm mark
questions.difficultyReason: The student must find field directions and compare the sums at different distances from the two wires.
questions.misconception: Adding field magnitudes where the fields oppose

explanation.body: By the right-hand grip rule, the fields add between the wires and oppose outside them. At the $40\ \mathrm{cm}$ mark, $B=\frac{\mu_0(2I)}{2\pi(0.10)}+\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi(0.20)}=\frac{12.5\mu_0 I}{\pi}$. At the $50\ \mathrm{cm}$ mark, $B=\frac{\mu_0(2I)}{2\pi(0.20)}+\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi(0.10)}=\frac{10\mu_0 I}{\pi}$. The greatest resultant is at $40\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: The weaker wire’s field opposes the stronger wire’s field at 20 cm.
perOption.B: Correct. The fields reinforce and the stronger wire is closer.
perOption.C: The fields reinforce, but the nearer wire carries the smaller current.
perOption.D: The two fields oppose at 70 cm, where the closer wire carries the smaller current.

questions.misconception: Using the field’s angle to the horizontal as its angle to the current.

explanation.body: The in-phase currents always flow in the same direction as each other whenever they are nonzero, so the force is attractive. The force is proportional to the product of the two equal currents, $F\propto\sin^2(2\pi t/T)$, so it repeats every $T/2$ at twice the current frequency.

They then enter a region of uniform magnetic field where P travels in a circular arc of radius 3.7 cm. uniform magnetic field velocity selector ions P and Q What is the radius of the circular arc travelled by ion Q? A 1.2 cm B 2.8 cm C 4.9 cm D 11 cm
questions.difficultyReason: The student must establish equal speeds before applying the mass-to-charge scaling for the radius.
questions.misconception: Treating the bending radius as proportional to charge.

explanation.body: In the selector, $B_1qv=qE$, so both ions emerge with speed $v=E/B_1$. In the second field, the magnetic force provides the centripetal force: $B_2qv=mv^2/r$, so $r=mv/(qB_2)=mE/(qB_1B_2)$. Therefore $r_Q=r_P(m_Q/m_P)(q_P/q_Q)=3.7(1/1.5)(2)=4.9\ \mathrm{cm}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Treats radius as proportional to charge as well as to mass.
perOption.B: Inverts the combined mass-to-charge ratio for Q relative to P.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses $m_P/m_Q$ where the conversion requires $m_Q/m_P$.

A current-carrying thin wire $30\ \mathrm{cm}$ long with a mass of $2.4\ \mathrm{g}$ is initially suspended at rest above the ground when placed in a uniform magnetic field of flux density $0.040\ \mathrm{T}$.

The wire experiences an upward acceleration of $1.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ when a current $I$ passes through it.

[A horizontal wire above the ground lies in a magnetic field directed into the page, shown by crosses.]

If the current in the wire is $\frac{I}{2}$, what will its acceleration be?

A. $0.60\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, upward
B. $4.3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, upward
C. $4.3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, downward
D. $5.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, downward

questions.difficultyReason: Requires finding the initial current and recalculating the signed net force at half that current.
questions.misconception: Halving net force when only magnetic force halves

explanation.body:
Taking upward as positive, $BIL\sin\theta-mg=ma$. Initially, $0.040I(0.30\sin90^\circ)-0.0024(9.81)=0.0024(1.2)$, giving $I=2.202\ \mathrm{A}$.

At half the current, $0.040(1.101)(0.30\sin90^\circ)-0.0024(9.81)=0.0024a$. Thus $a=-4.305\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, or $4.3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ downward.

perOption.A: Halves the original acceleration even though weight stays the same.
perOption.B: Reverses the direction of the net force, which points downward once weight exceeds magnetic force.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the magnetic force per unit mass as the magnitude of the net acceleration.

[Two vertical wires intersect the horizontal dashed line OX. P is on the left with an upward current arrow and Q is on the right with a downward current arrow. The horizontal separation is labelled $d$.]

What is the distance of this point from P?

questions.difficultyReason: Determine which side permits cancellation and use the two different distances in the field equation.
questions.misconception: Equating field magnitudes where both fields point the same way

explanation.body: The currents run in opposite directions, so the fields point the same way between the wires and can only cancel outside. The cancellation point must be nearer the smaller current, so it lies to the right of Q. If its distance from P is $y$, its distance from Q is $y-d$. Equating the two field magnitudes gives $4.0/y=3.0/(y-d)$, so $y=4d$.

perOption.A: Between the wires the fields point the same way, so they add at this position.
perOption.B: This balances field magnitudes between the wires, where the fields reinforce each other.
perOption.C: To the left of P, P has both the larger current and the shorter distance, so its field is stronger.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Four particles independently move at the same speed in a direction perpendicularly to the same magnetic field.

Which particle is deflected the most?
questions.stemText: Four particles independently move at the same speed in a direction perpendicularly to the same magnetic field. Which particle is deflected the most? A A proton B An electron C A copper ion D A helium nucleus
questions.difficultyReason: Compare the curvature of particle paths using the mass-to-charge ratio.
questions.misconception: Comparing charge alone to predict deflection

explanation.body: For perpendicular motion, the magnetic force supplies the centripetal force, giving $r=mv/(|q|B)$. With the same $v$ and $B$ for all four particles, the electron has the smallest mass-to-charge-magnitude ratio and therefore the smallest radius and greatest deflection.

perOption.A: A proton has the same charge magnitude as an electron but a much larger mass.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: A copper ion has a much greater mass per unit charge magnitude than an electron.
perOption.D: A helium nucleus carries twice the electron’s charge magnitude but has a much greater mass per unit charge magnitude.

If the force per unit length between wire X and wire Y is F, what is the force per unit length acting on wire Z?

If the force per unit length between wire X and wire Y is F, what is the force per unit length acting on wire Z? A 0 B F C 2F D 3F

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The two current products, separations and force directions must all be compared.
questions.misconception: Ignoring force direction or wire separation

explanation.body: For a long straight wire, $B=\mu_0 I/(2\pi r)$, so for the adjacent wires X and Y the force per unit length $F$ is proportional to $2I^2/r$. On Z, X gives an attractive force per unit length proportional to $4I^2/(2r)$, equal to $F$, and Y gives a repulsive one proportional to $8I^2/r$, equal to $4F$. These act in opposite directions, so the resultant is $4F-F=3F$.

perOption.A: Assumes the opposing forces have equal magnitudes.
perOption.B: Counts only the attraction towards X.
perOption.C: Treats X and Z as adjacent, giving an attraction of $2F$ instead of $F$.
perOption.D: Correct.

The magnitude of the force due to the magnetic field acting on the charge at this instant is
A 0 N
B $\dfrac{\mu_0 Iqv}{2\pi d}$
C $\dfrac{\mu_0 Iqv}{\pi d}$
D $\dfrac{2\mu_0 Iqv}{\pi d}$

questions.difficultyReason: Must find the direction of the resultant field at the mid-point and see that $\sin\theta=0$ or $v$ is parallel to it.
questions.misconception: Assumes a field-perpendicular geometry and gives a non-zero force.

explanation.body:
By the right-hand grip rule, opposite currents give fields at the midpoint that point in the same direction, perpendicular to the plane of the wires, so the resultant flux density is perpendicular to the plane.

The velocity $v$ is also perpendicular to this plane, so it is parallel to the resultant flux density.

The magnetic force $F = Bqv\sin\theta = 0$ since $\theta = 0^\circ$.

perOption.A: Correct. $v$ is parallel to the resultant $B$ so $F=0$.
perOption.B: Uses the field of a single wire at distance $d/2$ with $F=Bqv$.
perOption.C: Assumes the field is perpendicular to $v$ and uses a single wire at distance $d$.
perOption.D: Adds both wires' fields as if the velocity were perpendicular to $B$.

questions.stem:
An electron enters the vacuum between two oppositely charged plates with velocity v. The electron is followed by an alpha particle moving with the same initial velocity as the electron. A uniform magnetic field is directed into the plane of the paper.

The electron’s path is undeflected. The path of the alpha particle will be
questions.stemText: An electron enters the vacuum between two oppositely charged plates with velocity v. The electron is followed by an alpha particle moving with the same initial velocity as the electron. A uniform magnetic field is directed into the plane of the paper. The electron’s path is undeflected. The path of the alpha particle will be A undeflected. B deflected upward. C deflected downward. D deflected into the plane of the paper.

options.label: D
options.text: deflected into the plane of the paper.

questions.difficultyReason: Velocity selector reasoning: spotting that charge and mass cancel.
questions.misconception: Thinking the heavier or oppositely charged particle must deflect

explanation.body:
The electron passes undeflected, so the electric force equals the magnetic force: $qE = Bqv$.

The charge $q$ cancels, so the condition $v = E/B$ does not depend on the mass or charge. The alpha particle also has the same $v$, and its electric and magnetic forces (both reversed in direction relative to the electron) still balance, so it is undeflected.

perOption.A: Correct. $v = E/B$ is independent of charge and mass.
perOption.B: Assumes the magnetic force exceeds the electric force for the positive alpha particle.
perOption.C: Assumes the electric force exceeds the magnetic force for the alpha particle.
perOption.D: Forces from these fields act in the plane of the page; none points into the page.

[Diagram: coil pivoted at its top, hanging at 30 degrees to the vertical; its lowest side lies between the N pole (above) and S pole (below); a horizontal magnetic force arrow points left from the lowest side; the weight 0.12 N acts downward at the coil's centre.] When a current of 0.40 A passes through the coil, it hangs at an angle 30 degrees to the vertical with its lowest side in the vertical magnetic field of a magnet. The weight of the coil is 0.12 N. What is the magnetic flux density of the field between the magnets? A 0.029 T; B 0.058 T; C 0.087 T; D 1.4 T.

questions.difficultyReason: Needs moments with correct perpendicular distances at an angle, combined with F = NBIL.
questions.misconception: Using the full coil length for the weight's moment arm instead of half.

explanation.body:
Take moments about the pivot (the top side). The magnetic force $F_B$ acts horizontally on the lowest side, at perpendicular distance $L\cos 30^\circ$ from the pivot; the weight acts at the centre, at perpendicular distance $\dfrac{L}{2}\sin 30^\circ$.

$F_B \times L\cos 30^\circ = 0.12 \times \dfrac{L}{2}\sin 30^\circ$

$50B(0.40)(60\times10^{-3})\cos 30^\circ = 0.12 \times \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 30^\circ$

$B = 0.029\ \mathrm{T}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Moments about the pivot with $F_B = NBIL$.
perOption.B: Twice the answer: omits the factor of one half for the weight acting at the centre.
perOption.C: Three times the answer; likely a wrong trigonometric ratio in the moments.
perOption.D: Ignores the moment arms and the number of turns.

Axes: x to the right, y up.] What is the sign of charge of the particle and the direction of electric field to be applied in the same region, for it to pass through with no deflection? A positive, +y; B positive, -y; C negative, +y; D negative, -y.

questions.difficultyReason: Requires Fleming's left-hand rule for a moving charge and remembering the electric force on a negative charge is opposite to the field.
questions.misconception: Forgetting that the force on a negative charge is opposite to the electric field.

explanation.body:
The force causing the deflection acts upwards, so the magnetic force is upwards.

Using Fleming's left-hand rule, the current is opposite in direction to the motion of the particle, so it must be negatively charged.

If the magnetic force is upwards, the electric force must be downwards. For a negative charge this means the electric field must be upwards (+y).

perOption.A: Positive charge is wrong: the magnetic force would then be downwards, not upwards.
perOption.B: Positive charge is wrong, and the field direction does not match either.
perOption.C: Correct. Negative charge; the field points +y so the force on the negative charge is -y.
perOption.D: Negative charge is right, but a -y field would give a +y electric force on a negative charge, adding to the magnetic force.

The direction of the magnetic field at the centre of the equilateral triangle is

explanation.body:
Each wire produces a field at the centre perpendicular to the line joining it to the centre, with directions given by the right-hand grip rule.

perOption.B: The vertical components of $B_Q$ and $B_R$ cancel by symmetry, so there is no upward resultant.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An electron is moving with speed v beside a current carrying wire as shown.

What is the direction of the magnetic force acting on the electron?
questions.stemText: An electron is moving with speed v beside a current carrying wire as shown. v current electron What is the direction of the magnetic force acting on the electron? A into paper B out of paper C vertically downwards D vertically upwards
questions.difficultyReason: Two direction rules in sequence plus reversing for the negative charge.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to reverse the current direction for a negative charge

explanation.body:
The electron moves to the left, so the equivalent conventional current (middle finger) is to the right.

Using the right-hand grip rule for the upward current in the wire, the magnetic field at the electron (left of the wire) is out of the paper.

Applying Fleming's left-hand rule with field out of the paper and conventional current to the right, the force on the electron is vertically downwards.

perOption.A: The force must be perpendicular to the field, which is into/out of the paper here, so it cannot be into the paper.
perOption.B: Out of the paper is the direction of the magnetic field at the electron, not of the force.
perOption.C: Correct. Field out of paper, conventional current to the right, so the force is downwards.
perOption.D: This is the force on a positive charge moving left; the electron's negative charge reverses it.

questions.stem:
A wire 30 cm long with a mass of 4.0 g, is placed on a horizontal platform in a magnetic field of flux density 0.040 T. The diagram shows the top view of the set-up. The current I in the wire is slowly increased until the wire starts to lift off from the platform when I = $I_{o}$.

top view

What is value of $I_{o}$?
questions.stemText: A wire 30 cm long with a mass of 4.0 g, is placed on a horizontal platform in a magnetic field of flux density 0.040 T. The diagram shows the top view of the set-up. The current I in the wire is slowly increased until the wire starts to lift off from the platform when I = Io. B 30° I top view What is value of Io? A 3.3 A B 6.5 A C 33 A D 65 A
questions.difficultyReason: Needs to realise the horizontal field gives a vertical force and use the 30° angle between wire and field.
questions.misconception: Ignoring the angle between the wire and the field

explanation.body:
For the wire to start to lift off, the magnetic force must equal the weight of the wire.

$mg = BIL\sin\theta$

$0.004(9.81) = 0.040(0.30)(\sin 30^\circ)\,I$

$I = 6.54 \approx 6.5\ \mathrm{A}$

perOption.A: Ignores the angle (takes $\sin\theta = 1$), giving 3.3 A.
perOption.B: Correct. $I = mg/(BL\sin 30^\circ) = 6.5\ \mathrm{A}$.
perOption.C: Uses 0.04 kg instead of 0.004 kg for 4.0 g and also ignores the $\sin 30^\circ$ factor.
perOption.D: Uses 0.04 kg instead of 0.004 kg for the 4.0 g mass.

A square wire frame, of negligible mass, is supported horizontally on a knife edge so that XY of the frame lies perpendicular to a pair of magnets of length $L$. Current $I$ flows in the wire frame, while a mass $m$ is hung at a distance $q$ from the knife edge. The wire frame is in equilibrium when XY is at distance $p$ from the knife edge.

[Side XY runs between two magnets over length $L$. The knife edge crosses the square frame parallel to XY. The mass $m$ hangs from the opposite side. The distances from XY to the knife edge and from the knife edge to the opposite side are $p$ and $q$, respectively. Current $I$ points right along the rear side and left along the front side.]

Which expression gives the magnetic flux density $B$ between the magnets?

A $\frac{mgq}{I(p+q)p}$
B $\frac{mq}{I(p+q)p}$
C $\frac{mgq}{ILp}$
D $\frac{mq}{ILp}$

stemImage.alt: Question 25: An experiment is conducted to determine the magnetic flux density of a pair of magnets using a current balance. A square wire frame, of negligible mass, is supp

questions.difficultyReason: The calculation combines magnetic force on a wire with the principle of moments.
questions.misconception: Using the full side length as the length in the field.

explanation.body: Take moments about the knife edge. At equilibrium the moment of the weight balances that of the magnetic force, so $(mg)q=(BIL)p$. Rearranging gives $B=\frac{mgq}{ILp}$.

perOption.A: Uses the whole side length $p+q$ as the length of wire in the field.
perOption.B: Uses the full side length $p+q$ and substitutes mass for weight.
perOption.C: Correct. The weight and magnetic force produce equal opposing moments.
perOption.D: Omits $g$ when converting the hanging mass to weight.

The diagram shows arrows representing the magnetic flux density B at the position of each wire and the magnetic force F on each wire. (magnetic flux density at X due to Y) (magnetic flux density at Y due to X) The current in wire Y is doubled. Which diagram best represents the magnetic flux density and forces? A  B  C  D

appearances.originalFile: grail:10487 YIJC 2023 H2Phy Prelim P1 Question Paper

questions.difficultyReason: Students must separate each wire's own field from the field acting on it, and apply Newton's third law to the forces.
questions.misconception: Thinking the wire with the larger current experiences the larger force

explanation.body:
If the current in Y is doubled, the B-field at X due to Y doubles. The B-field at Y due to X is unaffected.

The force on X doubles, because the field at X due to Y has doubled. The force on Y also doubles, because the current in Y has doubled. This agrees with Newton's third law.

So the diagram shows $2B_Y$, $B_X$ and $2F$ on each wire.

perOption.A: The forces are a Newton's third law pair, so the force on X must also be $2F$. Also, $B_Y$ should double.
perOption.B: The field at X due to Y should double to $2B_Y$, since Y's current doubled.
perOption.C: $B_X$ depends only on the current in X, so it stays $B_X$. The force on Y must also be $2F$.
perOption.D: Correct. Only Y's field doubles, and both forces double equally.

questions.difficultyReason: Standard application of forces between parallel currents with an inverse-distance comparison.
questions.misconception: Assuming equal and opposite forces on the two sides of the loop cancel

explanation.body:
Parallel wires with currents in opposite directions repel; with currents in the same direction they attract.

PS carries current opposite to XY (repulsion) and QR carries current in the same direction as XY (attraction). Since PS is nearer to XY than QR, the repulsion is greater than the attraction, so the loop moves away from the long wire (to the right).

perOption.A: Assumes the attraction on QR dominates, ignoring that the field is stronger closer to the wire.
perOption.B: Correct. The nearer side PS is repelled more strongly than the farther side QR is attracted.
perOption.C: The forces on PS and QR are both in the plane and perpendicular to XY, and the forces on PQ and SR cancel, so there is no turning effect about an axis parallel to XY.
perOption.D: Assumes the forces on PS and QR cancel, but they differ because the field falls off with distance.
